Day 03 — Data Manipulation

The tidyverse (dplyr), loading/storing data, ordering, transforming variables, missing values, merging, restructuring, and aggregation

Authors

Johann-Friedrich Salzmann

Joshua Elias Schmidt Rodrigues

Date

September 2, 2026

Package management

Same as every session: bootstrap pacman, then load the tidyverse.

if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")
Loading required package: pacman

p_load(tidyverse)

Aggregation: group_by(), mutate(), and summarize()

A small toy tibble makes it easy to see exactly what each verb does to every row. The animations below are by Andrew Heiss (CC BY 4.0) — watch the rows to see what each call actually does.

df <- tribble(
  ~cat1, ~cat2, ~x,
  "a",   "j",   1,
  "a",   "j",   2,
  "a",   "k",   3,
  "b",   "j",   4,
  "b",   "k",   5,
  "b",   "k",   6,
  "c",   "j",   7,
  "c",   "j",   8,
  "c",   "k",   9
)
df
# A tibble: 9 × 3
  cat1  cat2      x
  <chr> <chr> <dbl>
1 a     j         1
2 a     j         2
3 a     k         3
4 b     j         4
5 b     k         5
6 b     k         6
7 c     j         7
8 c     j         8
9 c     k         9

df() also happens to be a base R function (the F-distribution density) — naming our tibble df shadows it, harmless here since we never need that function, but worth knowing.

mutate(): adds a column, keeps every row

df |>
  mutate(y = x - min(x))
# A tibble: 9 × 4
  cat1  cat2      x     y
  <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 a     j         1     0
2 a     j         2     1
3 a     k         3     2
4 b     j         4     3
5 b     k         5     4
6 b     k         6     5
7 c     j         7     6
8 c     j         8     7
9 c     k         9     8

The following works, but doesn’t make much sense — an aggregate function like mean() inside mutate() just gets recycled into every row.

df |>
  mutate(avg = mean(x))
# A tibble: 9 × 4
  cat1  cat2      x   avg
  <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 a     j         1     5
2 a     j         2     5
3 a     k         3     5
4 b     j         4     5
5 b     k         5     5
6 b     k         6     5
7 c     j         7     5
8 c     j         8     5
9 c     k         9     5

summarize(): collapses all rows into one

We instead want summarize(), which collapses all rows into one — actual aggregation.

df |>
  summarize(avg = mean(x))
# A tibble: 1 × 1
    avg
  <dbl>
1     5

Multiple aggregations can be computed at once — this is exactly what the animation below shows.

df |>
  summarize(avg = mean(x), total = sum(x), n = n())
# A tibble: 1 × 3
    avg total     n
  <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1     5    45     9

group_by() alone changes nothing visible

It just tags the tibble with grouping metadata; ungroup() removes the tag again.

df |>
  group_by(cat2)
# A tibble: 9 × 3
# Groups:   cat2 [2]
  cat1  cat2      x
  <chr> <chr> <dbl>
1 a     j         1
2 a     j         2
3 a     k         3
4 b     j         4
5 b     k         5
6 b     k         6
7 c     j         7
8 c     j         8
9 c     k         9
df |>
  group_by(cat2) |>
  ungroup()
# A tibble: 9 × 3
  cat1  cat2      x
  <chr> <chr> <dbl>
1 a     j         1
2 a     j         2
3 a     k         3
4 b     j         4
5 b     k         5
6 b     k         6
7 c     j         7
8 c     j         8
9 c     k         9

group_by() + mutate(): still one row per row, computed per group

Same recycling behavior as before, now per group — each row gets its own group’s average.

df |>
  group_by(cat1) |>
  mutate(avg = mean(x))
# A tibble: 9 × 4
# Groups:   cat1 [3]
  cat1  cat2      x   avg
  <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 a     j         1     2
2 a     j         2     2
3 a     k         3     2
4 b     j         4     5
5 b     k         5     5
6 b     k         6     5
7 c     j         7     8
8 c     j         8     8
9 c     k         9     8
df |>
  group_by(cat1) |>
  mutate(y = x - min(x))
# A tibble: 9 × 4
# Groups:   cat1 [3]
  cat1  cat2      x     y
  <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 a     j         1     0
2 a     j         2     1
3 a     k         3     2
4 b     j         4     0
5 b     k         5     1
6 b     k         6     2
7 c     j         7     0
8 c     j         8     1
9 c     k         9     2

group_by() + summarize(): one row per group

df |>
  group_by(cat1) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(x), total = sum(x), n = n())
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  cat1    avg total     n
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 a         2     6     3
2 b         5    15     3
3 c         8    24     3

df |>
  group_by(cat2) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(x), total = sum(x), n = n())
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  cat2    avg total     n
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 j      4.4     22     5
2 k      5.75    23     4

Grouping by two variables collapses to one row per combination — summarize() only drops the innermost (last) group, so cat1 grouping survives and R warns about it; ungroup() removes it explicitly.

df |>
  group_by(cat1, cat2) |>
  summarize(avg = mean(x), total = sum(x), n = n()) |>
  ungroup()
`summarise()` has regrouped the output.
ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by cat1 and cat2.
ℹ Output is grouped by cat1.
ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(cat1, cat2))` for per-operation grouping
  (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  cat1  cat2    avg total     n
  <chr> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 a     j       1.5     3     2
2 a     k       3       3     1
3 b     j       4       4     1
4 b     k       5.5    11     2
5 c     j       7.5    15     2
6 c     k       9       9     1

Excel has no dedicated date type, so Date comes back as a full timestamp (<dttm>) instead of a plain <date> — a small quirk worth knowing about, not a bug.

Storing data works the same way, one write_*() per format — write_csv(), write_dta(), write_sav(); Excel needs the writexl package. This is how polls_sample.* were produced, kept here for reference:

p_load(writexl)
polls_sample <- polls |> slice_head(n = 15)
write_dta(polls_sample, "polls_sample.dta")
write_sav(polls_sample, "polls_sample.sav")
write_xlsx(polls_sample, "polls_sample.xlsx")

Sums and means of booleans

A logical condition inside summarize() is just a column of TRUE/FALSE — sum() counts the TRUEs, mean() gives the proportion that are TRUE.

polls |>
  summarize(
    n_above_20 = sum(SPD > 20)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  n_above_20
       <int>
1        430

Other columns in polls do have missing values (e.g. FDP, Linke), so na.rm is worth adding as a habit — same as anywhere else it’s needed.

sum(1, 2, 3, NA)
[1] NA
sum(1, 2, 3, NA, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 6
polls |>
  summarize(
    n_above_20 = sum(SPD > 20, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_above_20 = mean(SPD > 20, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  n_above_20 pct_above_20
       <int>        <dbl>
1        430        0.207

Same idea, grouped — how often each pollster puts AfD above 25% in 2026.

polls |>
  filter(Date >= as.Date("2026-01-01")) |>
  group_by(Pollster) |>
  summarize(pct_afd_above_25 = mean(AfD > 25, na.rm = TRUE))
# A tibble: 8 × 2
  Pollster                pct_afd_above_25
  <chr>                              <dbl>
1 Allensbach                         0.5  
2 Forsa                              0.667
3 Forschungsgruppe Wahlen            0.727
4 GMS                                0.75 
5 INSA                               0.855
6 Infratest dimap                    0.429
7 Verian                             0.375
8 YouGov                             0.714

Selecting variables

select() takes a subset of columns, and can also be used to drop specific columns.

polls |>
  select(Pollster, Date, Period)
# A tibble: 2,077 × 3
   Pollster        Date       Period       
   <chr>           <date>     <chr>

 2 Infratest dimap 2017-01-05 02.01.–04.01.
 3 Verian          2017-01-07 03.01.–05.01.
 4 Forsa           2017-01-11 02.01.–06.01.

case_when() recodes a variable into categories, checked top to bottom — the first matching condition wins. Here: which Bundestag term a poll falls into, from its date.

polls_with_terms <- polls |>
  mutate(
    term = case_when(
      Date < as.Date("2021-10-26") ~ "19. Wahlperiode",
      Date < as.Date("2025-03-25") ~ "20. Wahlperiode",
      .default = "21. Wahlperiode"
    )
  )

coalesce() picks the first non-missing value across several columns, left to right — handy when the same information was collected repeatedly and you just want whichever answer came in.

survey_waves <- tribble(
  ~Respondent_ID, ~Response_May, ~Response_June, ~Response_July,
  1,              "CDUCSU",      NA,             "Gruene",
  2,              NA,            "FDP",          NA,
  3,              NA,            NA,             "AfD",
  4,              NA,            NA,             NA
)
survey_waves |>
  mutate(Latest_Response = coalesce(Response_July, Response_June, Response_May))
# A tibble: 4 × 5
  Respondent_ID Response_May Response_June Response_July Latest_Response
          <dbl> <chr>        <chr>         <chr>         <chr>          
1             1 CDUCSU       <NA>          Gruene        Gruene         
2             2 <NA>         FDP           <NA>          FDP            
3             3 <NA>         <NA>          AfD           AfD            
4             4 <NA>         <NA>          <NA>          <NA>

Real surveys often encode different kinds of missingness as sentinel numbers instead of leaving the cell blank. Same shape and entries as survey_waves above, but every non-response was coded with a number instead: 97 means “still undecided” (an actual answer worth keeping), 98/99 mean “don’t know”/“refused” (true missingness).

survey_sentinels <- tribble(
  ~Respondent_ID, ~Response_May, ~Response_June, ~Response_July,
  1,              "CDUCSU",      "99",           "Gruene",
  2,              "98",          "FDP",          "97",
  3,              "97",          "98",           "AfD",
  4,              "99",          "97",           "98"
)

~ .x is shorthand for a one-off function(x) ... — anonymous functions are covered properly on Day 4, previewed here since across() needs one to apply the same recoding to several columns at once. replace_values() only touches the values named on the left of each formula — everything else passes through unchanged.

survey_sentinels |>
  mutate(
    across(
      starts_with("Response"), ~ replace_values(
        .x,
        c("98", "99") ~ NA,
        "97"          ~ "Undecided"
      )
    )
  )
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  Respondent_ID Response_May Response_June Response_July
          <dbl> <chr>        <chr>         <chr>        
1             1 CDUCSU       <NA>          Gruene       
2             2 <NA>         FDP           Undecided    
3             3 Undecided    <NA>          AfD          
4             4 <NA>         Undecided     <NA>

Needing across() to mutate several look-alike columns the same way is itself a hint that the data would rather be long — one column, one mutate(), no across()/starts_with() needed at all.

survey_sentinels |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("Response"), names_to = "wave", values_to = "response") |>
  mutate(response = replace_values(response, c("98", "99") ~ NA, "97" ~ "Undecided"))

Restructuring data: pivot_longer() and pivot_wider()

One row per poll x party (long) instead of one row per poll (wide) — this is the reshaping step Day 2’s polls.csv already came pre-made from. Long format is what most tidyverse tools actually want: ggplot2 needs one column to map color/fill to (Day 2’s party colors), group_by()/summarize() need the grouping variable to be an actual column rather than spread across many columns, and joins match on a single key column the same way.

polls_long <- polls |>
  pivot_longer(CDUCSU:BSW, names_to = "party", values_to = "share")

Merging data: bind_rows() and joins

bind_rows() stacks tibbles with the same columns on top of each other. Filtering by party is only possible now that party is a column (long format) — in the wide file, each row already holds every party at once.

Joins add columns from a second table by matching a key — here, each party’s group in the European Parliament (2024–2029 term). Two mismatches on purpose: BSW isn’t in party_ep_groups (no match on the left), and Die PARTEI (a real party, one EP seat, “Non-attached” — not tracked by the Bundestag polling data) isn’t in polls_long (no match on the right), so all four join types actually differ from each other.

party_ep_groups <- tribble(
  ~party,   ~ep_group,
  "CDUCSU", "EPP",
  "SPD",    "S&D",
  "Gruene", "Greens/EFA",
  "FDP",    "Renew Europe",
  "Linke",  "The Left",
  "AfD",    "ESN",
  "DIE PARTEI", "Non-attached"
  # no BSW
)

# just the most recent polling day (2 polls x 7 parties = 14 rows) — small
# enough to actually see every join's differences, not just row counts
recent_polls_long <- polls_long |> filter(Date == max(Date))

Try it: Green vote share by Bundestag term

Your task: compute the Greens’ average polled vote share within each Bundestag term (Wahlperiode), ranked from highest to lowest — starting fresh from polls, not the term/long objects already built above.

polls |>
  pivot_longer(CDUCSU:BSW, names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(
    term = case_when(
      Date < as.Date("2021-10-26") ~ "19. Wahlperiode",
      Date < as.Date("2025-03-25") ~ "20. Wahlperiode",
      .default = "21. Wahlperiode"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(party == "Gruene") |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarize(avg_share = mean(share, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_share))
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  term            avg_share
  <chr>               <dbl>
1 19. Wahlperiode      16.7
2 20. Wahlperiode      15.6
3 21. Wahlperiode      12.2

Try it: which pollster shows AfD above 20% most often?

Your task: starting fresh from polls again, work out what share of each pollster’s polls put AfD above 20%, ranked from most to least often.

polls |>
  pivot_longer(CDUCSU:BSW, names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  filter(party == "AfD") |>
  group_by(Pollster) |>
  summarize(pct_above_20 = mean(share > 20, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_above_20))

Try it: rebuild Day 2’s polling trend plot

Your task: rebuild Day 2’s “color scales” plot, but starting straight from the wide polls tibble instead of an already-long one — there’s no one column called party to hand to color = here, only 7 separate share columns.

party_colors <- c(
  CDUCSU = "#000000",
  SPD    = "#E3000F",
  Gruene = "#46962b",
  FDP    = "#ffed00",
  Linke  = "#be3075",
  AfD    = "#009ee0",
  BSW    = "#7d3f98"
)

polls |>
  pivot_longer(CDUCSU:BSW, names_to = "party", values_to = "share") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = share, color = party)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = party_colors) +
  labs(title = "Bundestag polling trend", x = NULL, y = "Share (%)", color = "Party")
`geom_smooth()` using method = 'gam' and formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'

Warning: Removed 1548 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_smooth()`).

Try it: AfD vs. SPD — a negative correlation

Your task: check whether AfD and SPD support move in opposite directions — a Day 2 question, worth revisiting now that pivot_wider() is fresh. Pair each poll’s AfD and SPD share into one row per poll, then plot one against the other, overall and split out by year.

afd_spd <- polls_long |>
  filter(party %in% c("AfD", "SPD")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = party, values_from = share) |>
  mutate(year = year(Date))
